<reason>B wins by distinguishing intelligence establishing a dangerous situation from evidence identifying an individual carrier, thereby explaining what expansion adds. B also directly answers the revocation challenge with an explicit stopping rule. A’s strongest argument—that trust damage can precede review—creates a meaningful cost, but its claims of immediate cooperation collapse and inevitable repeated deployment are insufficiently supported. B’s closing supplies the better comparison: both missed interception and damaged trust can cause irreversible harm, while safeguards constrain searches before deployment as well as afterward. A instead repeats an already-answered redundancy objection.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s response to the “existing powers with paperwork” argument is decisive: authorization concerns the operation, while reasonable suspicion concerns the individual. A’s observation that context can help officers develop suspicion never establishes that it will reveal a concealed carrier. B preserves this protective gap throughout the exchange.</best_rebuttal>
